solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: City function subsequently returned food (10)

indicatorNotes.returned: sent back, so the word runs the other way

blocks.note: to function = to go, as a machine does
then = subsequently
grub = food; 'returned' turns it round to BURG

annotation.surface: Some civic occasion followed by a meal being sent back to the kitchen.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Function' reads as a noun, a formal event, but it is the verb: a machine that functions goes.
annotation.definitionFit: The definition is plain geography: Gothenburg is a large port on Sweden's west coast.

entries.clue: Conservative dignitary uncovered old documents, reportedly (8)

indicatorNotes.uncovered: with its covering, the first and last letters, taken off
indicatorNotes.reportedly: as it is said, so go by the sound

blocks.note: a worthy is a dignitary; strip its outer letters from W-ORTH-Y
O = old, plus docs = documents, respelt to match the sound

annotation.surface: A Tory grandee who has dug up some old papers, according to reports.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital C makes 'Conservative' look like the party, but the definition is the plain adjective: traditional, conventional.
annotation.definitionFit: Orthodox views are conventional, conservative ones.

entries.clue: Aspire to shorten first part of track and field event (3)

annotation.definition: first part of track and field event

indicatorNotes.to shorten: cut short, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: to aspire = to hope; shortened, HOPE loses its E

annotation.surface: An athlete hoping to trim the opening stretch of some track and field event.
annotation.walkthrough: The event is the triple jump, once called the hop, skip and jump, whose first phase is the hop.
annotation.definitionFit: The triple jump opens with a hop, then a step, then a jump.

entries.clue: Only performs with new material (5)

indicatorNotes.performs: acts on the letters, working them into a new order

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
the letters of ONLY rearranged

annotation.surface: A performer who only works when given new material to use.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Material' looks like a comedian's script, which is where the surface points; here it is fabric.
annotation.definitionFit: Material here is fabric, and nylon is the synthetic fibre woven into it.

entries.clue: Content of putrid, cold ulcer regularly ignored in part of ear (7)

indicatorNotes.Content of: what is inside, so the word without its first and last letters

blocks.note: the inside of p-UTRI-d
standard abbreviation, as on a tap
drop U, C and R from ULCER to leave L and E

annotation.surface: An ugly medical complaint: a festering cold sore somewhere in the ear.
annotation.walkthrough: Three selections are chained together; 'regularly ignored' keeps the second and fourth letters of ULCER, not the first and third.
annotation.definitionFit: The utricle is a small sac in the inner ear that senses balance.

entries.clue: Eatery harbours a penetrating germ on the counter (9)

indicatorNotes.penetrating: going inside, so these letters sit within the next word
indicatorNotes.on the counter: counter as in counter-clockwise: the letters run the opposite way

blocks.note: a bug is a germ; PORTS A goes inside it, after the U
harbours = ports, plus A used literally

annotation.surface: Restaurant inspectors warn of a bug lurking on the bar counter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Harbours' looks like the verb telling you something is hidden, and 'counter' looks like the bar top; both are wordplay, the first a noun and the second the reversal.
annotation.definitionFit: A gastropub is a pub that serves restaurant-quality food.

entries.clue: Desire sex next to church (4)

blocks.note: 'it' = sex appeal, or sex itself
standard abbreviation

annotation.surface: Lust stirring right beside the church.
annotation.walkthrough: 'It' for sex, as in having 'it', is an old crossword staple.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: having an itch to do something is wanting to do it.

entries.clue: Fanatical about volatile cleaner’s bigotry (11)

indicatorNotes.volatile: unstable, so the letters fly apart and re-form

blocks.note: to be into something is to be keen on it
the letters of CLEANER rearranged

annotation.surface: A cleaner with a hot temper and fixed prejudices.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Volatile' reads as the cleaner's temper; it is the instruction to rearrange CLEANER.
annotation.definitionFit: Intolerance of other people's views is bigotry.

entries.clue: Run into trees, and be unable to stop laughing (6)

indicatorNotes.into: 'Run into' is to collide with, and the R runs into the trees, ending up inside them

blocks.note: standard abbreviation, as on a cricket scorecard
a copse is a small wood

annotation.surface: Someone crashes into the trees and then cannot stop giggling.
annotation.walkthrough: To corpse is theatre slang for an actor breaking into uncontrollable laughter on stage; the grim noun sense is the one that springs to mind first.
annotation.definitionFit: An actor who corpses cannot stop laughing mid-scene.

entries.clue: Painter’s second drink ending in disaster (8)

indicatorNotes.ending in: the last letter of the word that follows

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
a tipple is a drink
the last letter of disasteR

annotation.surface: An artist's second drink, and things go badly wrong.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Painter's' pretends the second drink belongs to the painter; the apostrophe-s is just 'is' joining definition to wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A stippler paints with small dots or dabs.

entries.clue: Go after South American’s heavenly body (6)

blocks.note: S = South, A = American
a go = a turn; 'after' puts it behind SA

annotation.surface: Taking a turn after a South American traveller, gazing at the stars.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Go' reads as a verb but is the noun: your go in a game is your turn.
annotation.definitionFit: By example: Saturn is one of the planets, which older English calls heavenly bodies.

entries.clue: One who’s gone home, leaving home later than Charlie (6)

indicatorNotes.later than: coming after in time, so the leaving-home letters follow Charlie's

blocks.note: C is Charlie in the phonetic alphabet
off = leaving, departing, plus in = at home

annotation.surface: Someone heading off from home at a later hour than their friend Charlie.
annotation.walkthrough: To have gone home is a euphemism for having died, so the definition is the final home of one who has gone.
annotation.definitionFit: A coffin is where the dead person, one who has 'gone home', lies.

entries.clue: Maybe circles princess in dance on ice? (6-5)

blocks.note: circles are an example of figures, shapes
Kate, Princess of Wales

annotation.surface: A princess twirling round and round in some ice-dance routine.
annotation.walkthrough: The circles are also the figures of eight a skater traces, so the wordplay belongs in the picture.
annotation.definitionFit: To figure-skate is to glide through set patterns and moves on ice.

entries.clue: Slapdash stroke across second and third in Gleneagles (8)

indicatorNotes.across: stretching over, so it holds the other letters
indicatorNotes.second and third in: the letters in positions two and three of the next word

blocks.note: to stroke = to caress
g-LE-neagles

annotation.surface: A sloppy golf shot played at Gleneagles.
annotation.walkthrough: Gleneagles is a famous Scottish golf resort, which is why 'stroke' reads as a golf shot; it is a caress.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: slapdash and careless both mean done without due care.

entries.clue: Rogue helpers upset homeless person (5,7)

indicatorNotes.upset: knocked over, the letters tumbling into a new order

blocks.note: all twelve letters rearranged

annotation.surface: Crooked volunteers causing distress to someone living on the streets.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rogue helpers' reads as one phrase, but every letter is fodder and 'upset' is the only instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A rough sleeper is a homeless person who sleeps outdoors.

entries.clue: Sordid aspect of naval weapons close to Belarus (9)

indicatorNotes.close to: the close, the end, of the next word

blocks.note: mines laid at sea
the last letter of BelaruS

annotation.surface: A shady side to the navy's weapons deployed near Belarus.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Close to' looks like a place, near the Belarusian border, but means the end of the word.
annotation.definitionFit: Seaminess is the sordid, disreputable side of something.

entries.clue: Writes about square hills (8)

blocks.note: pens = writes
nine is a square number, three times three

annotation.surface: An author writing about some flat-topped hills.
annotation.walkthrough: The Pennines are a chain of hills in northern England. 'Square' is a noun here, a square number.
annotation.definitionFit: The Pennines are the upland range running down northern England.

entries.clue: Lecturer collects a scrap item of old farmyard machinery (6,6)

indicatorNotes.collects: gathers in, holding the other letters

blocks.note: a reader is a senior university lecturer
a = per, as in 'twice a day'
to bin = to scrap

annotation.surface: A lecturer who collects old farm machinery as scrap.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A' does not stay A: it is PER, as in ten pounds a head. Reader is a British academic rank just below professor.
annotation.definitionFit: A reaper-binder was a horse-drawn machine that cut corn and tied it into sheaves.

entries.clue: Former Queen Elizabeth’s introduction confused a loner (7)

indicatorNotes.introduction: the first letter, which introduces the word
indicatorNotes.confused: muddled, the letters in a new order

blocks.note: the first letter of Elizabeth
the letters of A LONER rearranged

annotation.surface: The late Queen Elizabeth muddled a solitary person when introduced to them.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Former Queen Elizabeth' reads as one royal name; the break comes after 'Queen'. Eleanor of Aquitaine and Eleanor of Castile were English queens.
annotation.definitionFit: Several medieval English queens were called Eleanor.

entries.clue: Protective equipment started to hold line (6)

blocks.note: to start, as a horse does, is to shy
standard abbreviation

annotation.surface: Safety gear was issued so that the line would hold.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Started' means began on the surface; in the wordplay it is jumped in fright, as a horse shies.
annotation.definitionFit: By example: a shield is the oldest piece of protective kit, held up against blows.

entries.clue: Pursue around St Ives, primarily to rebuke (8)

indicatorNotes.primarily: 'primarily' means first of all, so only the first letter of Ives counts

blocks.note: to chase = to pursue
ST as printed, plus the first letter of Ives

annotation.surface: Chasing someone round the Cornish seaside town of St Ives to tell them off.
annotation.walkthrough: St Ives is a Cornish seaside town; ST stays as printed and only Ives is cut to its first letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to chastise and to rebuke both mean to tell someone off.

entries.clue: Predecessor of King George IV rebuffed capital (6)

indicatorNotes.rebuffed: pushed back, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: Queen Anne reigned just before George I
used as printed

annotation.surface: The heir before George IV being turned away from London.
annotation.walkthrough: 'King George IV' reads as one monarch; split it, and the predecessor is of George I, who followed Queen Anne in 1714. The Roman IV is taken as letters.
annotation.definitionFit: By example: Vienna is Austria's capital city.

entries.clue: Church official cut grass next to road (5)

indicatorNotes.cut: trimmed, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: the church caretaker who leads processions and shows people to pews; 'cut' takes off the last letter

annotation.surface: A churchwarden mowing the grass alongside the road.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cut' sits happily with the grass, which is why it looks like mowing rather than the trimming instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A British regional sense: the verge is the grassy edge of a road, the shoulder to American drivers.

entries.clue: King and jack, perhaps, or two other high cards? (6)

blocks.note: the first of two more high cards: a ten
the second: an ace

annotation.surface: A card player weighing up holding king and jack or another high pair.
annotation.walkthrough: A tenace, in bridge and whist, is two cards in a suit with a gap between them, such as king and jack or ace and queen.
annotation.definitionFit: King and jack in one suit, missing the queen, form a tenace.

entries.clue: French commune organised retrospective — good for them! (8)

indicatorNotes.retrospective: looking back, so the word runs backwards

blocks.note: to organise an event is to run it; 'retrospective' flips RAN
good, in the language of the French just named

annotation.surface: A French town has put on a retrospective exhibition, and good for them!
annotation.walkthrough: 'Retrospective' looks like the exhibition that was organised; it is the reversal. Narbonne is a town in southern France.
annotation.definitionFit: Narbonne is a commune, a municipality, in the south of France.

entries.clue: Periodically used social lubricant (3)

blocks.note: the even letters of sOcIaL

annotation.surface: A drink now and then to ease people along at a party.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Social lubricant' is a stock phrase for alcohol, so the eye reads it whole; the break comes between the two words.
annotation.definitionFit: The surface phrase 'social lubricant' means drink; the definition takes the literal slippery sense, and oil is its prime example.

entries.clue: Smackhead zealously guards cutting tool (4)

indicatorNotes.guards: to guard is to keep something inside a protected space, so the answer is held within these words

blocks.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

annotation.surface: A heroin addict fiercely protecting a blade.
annotation.walkthrough: A smackhead is slang for a heroin addict.
annotation.definitionFit: An adze is an axe-like tool for shaping wood.

entries.clue: County snubbed very famous artist, possibly (10)

indicatorNotes.snubbed: cut short, like a snub nose, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: SURREY, the county south of London, without its Y
A-list celebrities are the most famous

annotation.surface: A county cold-shouldering a celebrated painter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Snubbed' reads as the county slighting the artist; it is the instruction to dock SURREY's tail.
annotation.definitionFit: A surrealist, such as Dalí or Magritte, is one kind of artist.
